blocks.text: Now I shall add something about the Hebrews, for the most learned of whom יענה jaana is the ostrich. That it is so taken is clear from Maimonides in the treatise On Forbidden Foods, at the beginning of chapter 3. And from the Glossators of the Talmud, who explain נעמיות naamijoth, that is, ostriches, [II, 820] by בנות יענה. So also Abraham Peritsol and Chazkuni on Leviticus explain it. And David de Pomis in his Lexicon says so most plainly, as if from Aben Ezra: יענה לפר׳ אברהם אע״ איוב לט״ הוא עוף אשר ישים ביצותיו בארץ ונקרא סטרו״צו בלעז, jaana, according to R. Abraham Aben Ezra on Iob. XXXIX., is a bird which lays its eggs on the ground, and in the vernacular is called struzzo, that is, in Italian. And the Porta coeli, fol. 22. d.: ומין אחד מן בח״ שהוא אמצעי בין חיה ועוף והוא בת־יענה שאינו מעופף ואינו הולכת אך יש לה חרודים תחת כנפיה ועוקצתם אותה והוא מדלגת ומאכלה הברזל ואומרים עליה כי בראיה תאסיף ביציה וכתב אבן רשד כי בהלעיטה את הזהב הוא נתך בגופה מחממה יותר מן האש בסגולה שלהם, There is one species of animal intermediate between quadrupeds and birds, namely bath-jaana, which neither flies nor walks, but has spikes under its wings, by which it is pricked, and it leaps. It also feeds on iron, and is said to hatch its eggs by looking at them. Averroës writes that it melts swallowed gold in its body by its heat better than fire does, and this by a certain innate power. Repeating this last point at fol. 23. b., the same work has הנעמיות in place of daughters of jaana. Thus for him בת־יענה, daughter of jaana, and נעמית naamith are synonyms, and both mean the ostrich. Nor do we find any of the Hebrews who interprets it otherwise. For Kimchi and others, who hold that יענה jaana is a θρηνητικὴν [thrēnētikēn] bird, nevertheless do not deny that it is the ostrich.
